title: dig follow-up: radblok.co.za is hosted on Render, not xneelo
summary: Three dig commands to follow up on theHarvester's mail.radblok.co.za finding. MX record confirmed, IP confirmed, but the reverse DNS was the surprise: 216.24.57.1 belongs to Render.com — a cloud hosting platform — not xneelo. This corrects the assumption from Entry 006 that xneelo was the hosting provider. Nameservers and hosting are two different things.

sections.h: The three commands and their output

blocks.label: kali
blocks.text:
$ dig radblok.co.za MX +short
10 mail.radblok.co.za.

$ dig mail.radblok.co.za A +short
216.24.57.1

$ dig -x 216.24.57.1 +short
ip-216-24-57-1.ingress.render.com.

head: Part
Meaning
rows: **Priority** — when multiple MX records exist, lower number = higher priority. A single record means all mail goes here.
**Mail exchanger** — the hostname that receives inbound email for the domain. The trailing dot is standard DNS notation for a fully-qualified domain name.

blocks.text: The MX record points to `mail.radblok.co.za` — a subdomain of the same domain. That subdomain resolves to `216.24.57.1`. So all email to `@radblok.co.za` gets routed to that IP.

`dig -x` does a **PTR lookup** — the reverse of a normal A lookup. Instead of 'what IP does this hostname resolve to', it asks 'what hostname does this IP reverse to'. The answer: `ip-216-24-57-1.ingress.render.com` — which is **Render.com's infrastructure**, not xneelo.

**Render** is a cloud application hosting platform (similar to Heroku or Railway). The `ingress` part of the hostname is Render's load-balancer layer — the entry point that receives traffic and routes it to the deployed application. This IP is one of Render's shared ingress nodes.

**This corrects Entry 006.** The assumption there was: 'nameservers are xneelo, therefore xneelo is the hosting provider.' That was wrong. xneelo manages the **DNS** (nameservers, whois, domain registration). The actual **application** runs on Render. These are two completely separate providers.

This is a common real-world split: one company handles domain registration and DNS, a completely different company hosts the actual application. You see this constantly — Cloudflare for DNS, AWS for hosting; GoDaddy for the domain, Vercel for the app. **whois nameservers only tell you who manages DNS. They say nothing about where the application runs.**

The recon lesson: whois → nameservers → hosting is a **faulty assumption**. The correct chain is: whois gives you the registrar and nameservers; `dig A` gives you the IP; `dig -x` gives you the actual hosting provider. All three steps are needed to get the full picture.
The MX record pointing to a Render IP is unusual. Render is a web app platform — it doesn't run traditional mail servers (SMTP daemons, mailboxes). Likely scenarios:

items: The app hosted on Render handles inbound email programmatically — e.g. via a webhook from a mail service like SendGrid or Mailgun, which receives the mail and forwards parsed data to the app.
The `mail.radblok.co.za` A record was set up to point to the app server, and the MX record followed — not a traditional mail server, but a web endpoint that processes mail.
Or the MX / mail subdomain is a leftover / placeholder that doesn't have an active mail daemon listening.

blocks.text: To confirm: a port scan of `216.24.57.1` on ports 25 (SMTP), 465 (SMTPS), 587 (submission) would tell you immediately whether a real mail service is listening there — or whether it's just a web server on 80/443.

items: Reverse DNS on `216.24.57.1`: **Render.com ingress** — not xneelo.
Corrected Entry 006 assumption: xneelo = DNS only; Render = actual hosting.
Practical lesson: whois nameservers ≠ hosting provider. Always `dig A` then `dig -x`.
Mail setup on Render is unusual — needs a port scan to confirm what's actually listening.
Next: `nmap -sV -p 25,80,443,465,587 216.24.57.1` to see what services are running on the Render node (only do this against infrastructure you own or are authorised to scan).
